bib.title: RAT: Retrieval Augmented Thoughts Elicit Context-Aware Reasoning in Long-Horizon Generation

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "RAT: Retrieval Augmented Thoughts Elicit Context-Aware Reasoning in Long-Horizon Generation", Zihao Wang, Anji Liu, Haowei Lin, Jiaqi Li, Xiaojian Ma, Yitao Liang (PKU, UCLA, BIGAI). arXiv:2403.05313v1, preprint, March 2024.

COVERAGE: 25 pages. About 79,000 of 90,697 chars read: pp. 1-10 main text, limitations, ethics, the reference list (skimmed), and appendices A (tasks), B (prompts), C (TrueSkill), D (contamination), and E.1 (Minecraft case plus Table 6). Not read: the tail of appendix E.2, which holds only creative-writing example outputs (pp. ~22-25). Extraction was clean.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- RAT is a zero-shot prompting procedure. The model drafts a zero-shot CoT, then revises each thought step in order. For step i it retrieves with a query built from the task prompt, the already-revised steps T*_1:i-1 and the current draft step T_i. It then rewrites the step with the retrieved text in context and appends the next draft step.
  number: none
  setup: Algorithm 1, Sec 2.2. ToQuery is either a text encoder or an LLM. Code tasks embed the code draft directly. Planning and writing tasks use an extra LLM query-generation prompt.
  quote: "we devise a progressive approach, whereLLMs produce the response step-by-step following theCoT (a series of subtasks), and only the current thought step will be revised based on the information retrieved with task prompt, the current and the past CoTs."
  where: p.1 (intro); Algorithm 1 on p.4

- RAT beats plain RAG and zero-shot CoT on code generation across three models. The average pass@1 relative gain over DIRECT is 7.35% (CodeLlama-7b), 9.17% (GPT-3.5) and 13.63% (GPT-4).
  number: GPT-4 average pass@1 67.55% for RAT vs 59.45% DIRECT, 58.10% CoT, 60.86% RAG-1 and 61.50% RAG-5. GPT-4 HumanEval pass@1 is 69.33% vs 57.32% DIRECT (+20.94%).
  setup: Table 1. HumanEval (164 problems), HumanEval+, MBPP (index 11-175), MBPP+ (first 164). Zero-shot. Retrieval corpus is codeparrot/github-jupyter (452k markdown/code pairs). Embeddings from text-embedding-ada-002.
  quote: "GPT-4 RAT 69.33% 88.40% 64.63% 82.21% 68.90% 79.85% 67.36% 82.14% 67.55% 83.15%"
  where: Table 1, p.6

- On math, RAT gives a large relative gain on GSM-Hard. GSM8K and GSM-Hard are scored on GPT-3.5 with PAL-style program generation.
  number: GSM8K 71.36% vs 65.85% DIRECT. GSM-Hard 67.34% vs 51.26% DIRECT. Average 69.35% (+16.96%). CoT (zero-shot) is worse than DIRECT at 54.27%, which is -7.32 points. RAG-1 averages 56.54% and RAG-5 averages 59.30%.
  setup: Table 2. First 200 samples per benchmark, three attempts averaged, no in-context examples. The text separately says GPT-4 reaches a 10.26% relative improvement.
  quote: "RAT 71.36% 67.34% 69.35(+16.96)%"
  where: Table 2, p.6; Sec 3.5 p.9; Appendix A.2

- Embodied planning (Minecraft) shows the biggest gain. Executability goes from 19.33% (DIRECT) to 76.67% (RAT). Zero-shot CoT reaches 49.33%.
  number: Executability 76.67±8.02%. Plausibility rating 29.37 (+42.78% over DIRECT). The abstract's 42.78% is this plausibility rating gain.
  setup: GPT-4 base. 100 randomly chosen tasks in MC-TextWorld. Sources are Minecraft Wiki and DigMinecraft, chunked to at most 2000 tokens. Plausibility comes from human TrueSkill rating.
  quote: "RAT 71.36% 67.34% 69.35(+16.96)% 81.01% 29.07(+19.2%) 1.08 76.67±8.02% 29.37(+42.78%) 3.37"
  where: Table 2, p.6

- Creative writing: RAT has an 81.01% win rate against 46.67% for DIRECT. Its TrueSkill rating is 29.07, which is +19.2% over DIRECT's 24.39.
  setup: GPT-3.5. Three task types (survey, Jin Yong's life, American Civil War timeline), three variants each. Retrieval uses Google search. More than 10 human annotators per task group. RAG-1 and RAG-5 score below DIRECT on this task (23.99 and 23.88).
  quote: "RAT 71.36% 67.34% 69.35(+16.96)% 81.01% 29.07(+19.2%)"
  where: Table 2, p.6; Appendix A.4 and C

- Ablation 1: using the revised, partial thought as the query beats using the whole CoT as the query. The gain is a few points.
  number: HumanEval pass@1 is 50.6% baseline (RAG-1), 53.9% CoT+RAG and 59.2% RAT. pass@5 is 76.2%, 76.8% and 80.4%. CoT+RAG on HumanEval+ pass@5 is 69.3%, which is -1.2 points below baseline.
  setup: Table 3, GPT-3.5, HumanEval and HumanEval+.
  quote: "CoT+RAG 53.9(+3.3)% 76.8(+0.6)% 51.3(+3.1)% 69.3(-1.2)%"
  where: Table 3, p.8

- Ablation 2: the causal version (query from prior revised steps plus the current step) beats the non-causal version (the initial CoT retrieves everything at once). The gap is small.
  number: HumanEval pass@1 is 47.3% CoT baseline, 57.3% non-causal and 59.2% causal. pass@5 is 75.8%, 78.0% and 80.4%. HumanEval+ pass@5 is 74.8% non-causal vs 76.0% causal.
  setup: Table 4, GPT-3.5, CoT baseline.
  quote: "Non-Causal 57.3(+10.0)% 78.0(+2.1)% 54.9(+13.2)% 74.8(+0.0)%"
  where: Table 4, p.8

- Retrieval helps only if the base model can use the retrieved text. The largest gain was on GPT-4. The smallest model regressed on one benchmark.
  number: CodeLlama-7b MBPP+ pass@1 is 39.14% for RAT vs 41.22% DIRECT (-5.05%).
  setup: Sec 3.5, Table 1. The authors attribute this to weak in-context learning in small models. This is a hypothesis, not tested.
  quote: "On MBPP+, CodeLlama-7b basedRAT has demon-strated performance degradation. This decline could be due to the limited in-context learning ability of smaller language models."
  where: p.9

- Naive RAG and zero-shot CoT can underperform the plain model. Examples are CoT on code (GPT-3.5 average pass@1 47.98% vs 53.59% DIRECT) and RAG-1/RAG-5 on GSM8K.
  number: GSM8K RAG-1 and RAG-5 are 61.81% vs 65.85% DIRECT.
  setup: Tables 1-2.
  quote: "RAG-1 shot 61.81% 51.26% 56.54(+4.17)%"
  where: p.6

- Retrieval-corpus fine-tuning is worse than RAT in context.
  number: CodeLlama-7B-Python on HumanEval pass@1 is 40.85% DIRECT, 29.02% FINETUNE and 45.73% RAT.
  setup: Table 5. A contamination check. Benchmark-matching code was removed from the corpus following Guo et al. (2024).
  quote: "DIRECT 40.85% 53.65% 37.43% 48.78%
FINETUNE 29.02% 40.24% 26.34% 35.98%
RAT 45.73% 59.75% 43.29% 53.66%"
  where: Table 5, p.20

- Why it works, the authors' hypothesis. Each step is revised separately, so already-correct steps are not corrupted. Retrieval for intermediate sub-questions is easier than for the final answer. Hallucinations are mostly in details such as dates, and these do not stop the search engine finding the right page. The authors support this with ablations and case studies, not a direct test.
  number: none
  quote: "Revising a complete CoT with RAG could introduce errors at otherwise already-correct steps."
  where: p.5; case analysis p.7-8 (draft said the Civil War began April 12, 1860; correct is 1861)

LIMITS
- The authors concede (p.10) that RAT depends on the base LLM's CoT and in-context (RAG) ability. They say the effect on weaker models such as GPT-2 "is questionable".
- Quality of the knowledge base matters. An irrelevant knowledge base gives unhelpful retrieval. A large knowledge base is costly to maintain and hurts retrieval precision.
- Step-by-step reasoning may be redundant for simple questions. Some tasks need tree or graph structures. The authors give no comparison with ToT.
- The paper does not report cost, latency or call counts. RAT needs roughly 1 retrieval and 1 revision call per step (n steps), plus a query-generation call on writing and planning tasks.
- Small test sets: math uses 200 samples, Minecraft uses 100 tasks, and the writing task has 9 prompts. Plausibility and writing scores come from human TrueSkill with no inter-annotator agreement reported. The Minecraft ± is large (±8.02%).
- Math uses PAL (program execution), not text CoT, so the zero-shot CoT row there is not pure text reasoning.
- The retrieval corpus is jupyter notebooks (for code and math), Minecraft wikis, or live Google. Gains depend on a corpus that contains the needed facts. Generalisation to other corpora is not shown.
- Only OpenAI GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 plus CodeLlama-7b were tested. The model versions are not given, and they have dated.
- Appendix B says Bing in the query prompt, while the setup says Google. This is a small inconsistency.
- The abstract's per-domain figures (13.63% code, 16.96% math, 19.2% writing, 42.78% planning) mix the best model (GPT-4 code), GPT-3.5 (math and writing) and GPT-4 (planning), and they are relative gains. Cite each with its setup. 13.63% is GPT-4 only; the other two code models gain 7.35% and 9.17%. The 42.78% is a plausibility rating gain, not executability.
- The text says GSM8K +8.36% in the intro and +8.37% in Sec 3.2, a small inconsistency. Table 2 shows 71.36 vs 65.85, which is 8.37% relative. The text's "18.44% average" for GSM conflicts with the table's +16.96% (the table is relative to the average; the 18.44% is the text's own figure and is not in the table).

BUILDS ON
Chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022); zero-shot CoT "let's think step by step" (Kojima et al., 2022); RAG (Lewis et al., 2020b); PAL (Gao et al., 2022); DEPS planning prompts (Wang et al., 2023c) and MC-TextWorld (Lin et al., 2023). Related work it contrasts with: IRCoT (Trivedi et al., 2022b), IRGR (Ribeiro et al., 2022), GEEK (Liu et al., 2023a), ITRG (Feng et al., 2023a), Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2023), Chain-of-Verification (Dhuliawala et al., 2023), least-to-most (Zhou et al., 2022a), self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022), Tree-of-Thought (Yao et al., 2023), Graph-of-Thought (Besta et al., 2023), STaR (Zelikman et al., 2022). Evaluation: HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), EvalPlus (Liu et al., 2023b), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), TrueSkill (Herbrich et al., 2006), contamination preprocessing (Guo et al., 2024).

CODE (Algorithm 1, p.4, verbatim)
1: T = {T1..Tn} <- p_theta(.|I)   (generate zero-shot initial step-by-step thoughts)
2: T* <- T1, i <- 1
3: repeat
4:   Q_i <- ToQuery(I, T*)   (generate query from current draft answer)
5:   R_i <- RetrieveFromCorpus(Q_i)
6:   T* <- p_theta(.|I, T*, R_i)   (revise draft answer based on retrieved text)
7:   T* <- CONCAT(T*, T_{i+1})
8:   i <- i+1
9: until i > n
10: return T*

Revision prompt (App. B.3, p.19), key lines: "You need to check whether the answer is correct. If you find some errors in the answer, revise the answer to make it better. If you find some necessary details are ignored, add it to make the answer more plausible according to the related text. If you find the answer is right and do not need to add more details, just output the original answer directly."
Query prompt (B.2): "I want to verify the content correctness of the given question, especially the last sentences. Please summarize the content with the corresponding question. This summarization will be used as a query..." and "Try to make the query as relevant as possible to the last few sentences in the content."

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): RAT pipeline. It shows the Minecraft "Mine 4 planks" step corrected to "Mine 4 logs" by retrieval, then step 2 revised with step 1 in context. It is the fastest way to see the loop.
- Fig 2 (p.3): Jin Yong example. DIRECT and CoT hallucinate (Cambridge graduation), RAG is too specific with a loose structure, RAT is accurate and complete. A bar chart (bottom) compares methods per task.
- Fig C.1 (p.20): human evaluation UI. Low value.
